To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

CLL cells infected ex-vivo with a recombinant MVA encoding for 3 costimulatory molecules are capable of stimulating proliferation of both allogenetic and autologous CD4+ and CD8+ T cells, and of inducing the generation of cytotoxic T lymphocytes against unmodified/un-infected CLL cells.

we have demonstrated that the simultaneous delivery of the costimulatory molecules B7-1, ICAM-1, and LFA-3 on CLL cells via infection of the CLL cells with a recombinant MVA vector, MVA-TRI COM, results in the generation of cytotoxic T lymphocytes that recognize and kill the autologous CLL cells.

we have developed an effective approach to immunotherapy for chronic lymphocytic lymphoma (CLL) by enhancing the immunogenicity of tumor cells via infection with recombinant vectors encoding for multiple co-stimulatory molecules.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a novel immunotherapy approach for patients with CLL.
developing a new therapeutic approach to CLL.

the development of a potential immunotherapy of CLL by using CLL cells as a vehicle to express multiple costimulatory signals to enhance the ability of the CLL cells to present tumor antigens to the autologous T cell.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
this is a very interesting and promising study that may have important implications for the immunotherapy and treatment of patients with CLL.
the results of this study demonstrate the feasibility of the use of CLL as a cellular vaccine in the immunotherapy of this disease.
the MVA-TRIOM vector is a promising candidate for the immunotherapy for CLL.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that CLL cells can be manipulated in vitro to express multiple costimulatory signals.
the simultaneous delivery of 3 costimulatory molecules, B7-1, LFA-3, and ICAM-1, on the surface of tumor cells via infection with MVA, results in the generation of tumor-specific CTLs.
we have demonstrated the ability of in vivo manipulated CLL cells, through hyperexpression of a trio of costimulatory proteins, to stimulate effective antileukemic T-cell responses.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we have shown for the first time that it is possible to infect CLL cells with MVA and to induce expression of costimulatory signals on the cell surface.

we can take CLL cells, a cell that is a bad antigen-presenting cell (APC) because they don't express the costimulatory molecules that are required for the activation of T cells, and by infecting them with a virus that can deliver these molecules, we can make these CLL cells into very effective antigen-presenting cells that can then stimulate T cells and induce an immune response against the CLL cells.
CLL cells can be used for the immunotherapy.
